unterschrift.text: After e2–e4 it covers d5 and f5 (gold). It will never be able to cover the squares d3 and f3 (red) again.

fragen.frage: What did the pawn give up behind it with the move e2–e4?
antworten: Nothing: it simply covers other squares now.
The squares d3 and f3: it will never cover them again, because pawns never move backward.
The squares d5 and f5.
fragen.erklaerung: In front, the pawn gains d5 and f5; behind, it loses d3 and f3 forever. Every pawn move is final.

aufgabe.text: Apply the protection test to the black pawns in

: Which pawns fail it, and which weakness from this chapter does each one have? Then count the pawn islands of both sides. Which side is structurally better according to the rule of thumb, and what does the other side have as compensation?

loesung.text: Two black pawns fail the protection test: the pawn on a7 is an
isolani
, since there is no black pawn left on the b-file. The pawn on c6 is
backward

: its neighbor d5 is already ahead of it, and there is no pawn on the b-file that could protect it. The pawn on d5, on the other hand, is healthy, because c6 protects it. The islands: Black has three (a7, c6–d5, and f7–h7), White only two (a2–c2 and f2–h2). According to the rule of thumb, White is therefore structurally better. In return, Black has the half-open b-file, on which a rook can put pressure on the pawn on b2, and active bishops. Remember: the protection test shows you which pawns will tie down pieces later.

erklaerung.text: a7 is an isolani, c6 a backward pawn; Black has three pawn islands, White two. White is structurally better; in return, Black has the half-open b-file against b2 and active bishops.

aufgabe.text: Which of the two black bishops in
is the “bad” one and which is the “good” one? Explain your answer. Which white bishop is bad by the same standard?

loesung.text: The bishop on f8, which travels on dark squares, is the bad bishop, since both d6 and e5 are dark squares and block its diagonals. The bishop on c8 is the good one, because the central black pawns do not stand on its light color: exactly the opposite of the French Advance Variation, where the light-squared bishop on c8 was the bad one. For White, d3 and e4 stand on light squares, so the light-squared bishop on f1 is the bad one. Remember: what decides is not the color of the bishop itself, but the color on which your own pawns stand.

erklaerung.text: The black pawns d6 and e5 stand on dark squares, so the dark-squared bishop on f8 is the bad one and c8 the good one. For White, d3 and e4 stand on light squares, which is why the bishop on f1 is the bad one.

aufgabe.text: Carry out the complete skeleton X-ray for the position in

: answer all four guiding questions for White and for Black, and then formulate a plan in one sentence for each side. Compare the result with the French Advance Variation from Section 5.7: where does the most important difference lie?

loesung.text: Squares:
The e5-pawn takes d6 and f6 away from Black, and the d5-pawn takes c4 and e4 away from White. There is no hole that either side could use immediately.
Pawns:

White's base d4 fails the protection test, since the c-pawn has been traded and the e-pawn already stands ahead of it. That is why the knights on b3 and f3, the bishop on e3, and the queen on d1 guard it. For Black, everything is healthy: d5 is protected by e6, e6 by f7. Both sides have two pawn islands.
Direction:
White's chain points to the kingside, and White has space there. Black's chain points to the queenside. The lever
has already been played, and Black is now pressing on d4 with pieces and using the open c-file.
Pieces:
The center is closed. Black's bishop on f5 stands
outside
the chain and is active. White's bishop on e3 stands on the color of its own chain, but is busy defending d4. The rooks of both sides belong on the open c-file.
Plans:

White: “I use my space on the kingside, fight for the open c-file, and secure my base d4 with pieces.” Black: “I use the open c-file and my active bishop on f5, attack the base d4, and secure my kingside.”
The most important difference
from the French Advance Variation lies in the fourth guiding question: Black has no locked-in bishop, because Black developed it before
. Remember: the same pawn structure can turn out quite differently for the pieces. That is why the fourth question is always part of it.

erklaerung.text: White's base d4 is weak and ties down pieces, and White has space on the kingside; Black presses against d4 via the open c-file. Unlike in the French Advance Variation, Black has no locked-in bishop, because Black developed it before ...e6.

text.text: d5 is a permanent hole in Black's camp, supported by the e4-pawn – an ideal square for a knight. The knight on c3 already guards it.

The e5-pawn takes the squares d4 and f4 away from White. There is no white hole that Black could use permanently. d5 is watched by the bishop on e6, the knight on f6, and later the knight on d7 via b6.

No white pawn can attack d5, in front of the isolani, anymore: the blockade square. Black already controls it with the bishop on b7, the knight on f6, and the pawn on e6.
d4 fails the protection test: no white pawn can ever protect it. Three pawn islands.
Healthy: b6 is protected by a7, e6 by f7. Two pawn islands.
